newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan closes troubled bank in new financial blow.
newsitem.headline: Japan closes troubled bank in new financial blow.

text.p: Japanese authorities ordered a troubled bank to halt business on Thursday -- the first time they have done so in five decades -- and won plaudits for quickly trying to head off a new financial embarrassment.

Finance Ministry figures showed Hanwa Bank Ltd suffocating under a heap of 190 billion yen ($1.71 billion) in problem loans, against its comparatively puny capital of 20.3 billion yen ($182 million) at the end of September.
In a scene now all too familiar, housewives, shopkeepers and students queued for two hours outside the bank's headquarters in the western Japanese town of Wakayama to withdraw their money.

It was only the third bank failure in Japan since the end of World War Two. There was one last year and one earlier this year. Eleven smaller credit unions and credit associations have also gone under since December 1994.
Like much of Japan's financial system, Hanwa was hard-hit by the collapse of property prices from the sky-high levels of the 1980s "bubble" era, when share prices also soared.

The bank's new president, Zenji Watanabe, told a news conference Hanwa's loans to the real estate sector were abnormally high, at about 30 percent of its lending, compared with only about 10 percent for other similar-sized banks.
The Finance Ministry said it had suspended operations at the second-tier regional bank, except for deposit withdrawals.
Finance Minister Hiroshi Mitsuzuka told a news conference, however, that the failure ought not to cause anxiety about Japan's financial system overall.
His ministry said swift handling of banking failures was essential for the recovery of Japan's financial system -- a view echoed by Bank of Japan Governor Yasuo Matsushita.

"The Bank of Japan believes that prompt measures to deal with insolvent financial institutions without delay will lead to the early rejuvenation of the functions of the Japanese financial system," he told a news conference.
Hanwa, employing 850 people at 53 branches handling one million accounts, operates mostly around the city of Osaka.
Finance Ministry officials said a new bank would be set up for the sole purpose of winding up Hanwa's business.
Financial analysts applauded the decision to wind up Hanwa -- without waiting for a run on the bank by depositors -- as a welcome sign after years of regulatory reluctance to act.

"I wouldn't characterise this as a banking problem, I would characterise this as beginning of a cleanup," said James McGuinness, an analyst at Dresdner Kleinwort Benson International. "This is what everyone has been wanting -- for them to take a proactive stance," he added.
Hanwa has book assets of about 658 billion yen ($5.92 billion). It is not one of Japan's top 20 commercial banks.

Hanwa, established in 1941, said on Thursday that it made a parent current loss of 33.72 billion yen ($303 million) in the six months to September 30. Two weeks ago, the bank forecast a loss of just 280 million yen ($2.52 million) for the period.
Last year, Japan suffered its first bank failure since the war when Hyogo Bank, also in western Japan, fell victim to bad loans. Another small regional bank went under this year.

Tokyo shares held steady, although some regional bank shares fell. The key Nikkei 225 average closed 0.22 percent lower at 21,143.34. Early gains in bond prices were offset by speculative selling, and Japanese government bonds ended lower.

The dollar was little affected in Tokyo trade, after news of Hanwa's failure helped limit its downside in New York on Wednesday. But the U.S. currency later edged up on talk that a major Japanese bank in New York might face problems.

An Asahi Bank spokesman told Reuters the bank was looking into a report by Kyodo news agency that its New York branch could face legal action for allegedly viewing a confidential Federal Reserve inspection report this summer. ($1=111 yen)
